tier_reason: docs/benchmarks/README.md gives the per-machine cost ratios against std::mt19937 produced by benchmarks/bench_engines.cpp (Google Benchmark, DoNotOptimize/ClobberMemory on the buffer). docs/benchmarks/raw/machines.csv records the compiler (GCC 13.3.0 on x86, GCC 12.2.0 on the Pi 5), the exact command and the CPU (e.g. Xeon Platinum 8481C, Cortex-A76). The bench preset is CMake Release plus per-kernel ISA flags in CMakeLists.txt.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.3.0 (Ubuntu 24.04) for every x86 matrix run and GCC 12.2.0 (Debian 12) for the Pi 5 NEON run (docs/benchmarks/raw/machines.csv); CMake 'bench' preset = CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release (CMake default -O3 -DNDEBUG for GCC), with kernel TUs adding -mavx2 or -mavx512f -mavx512dq -mavx512vl (CMakeLists.txt); runs through scripts/benchmarks/run_matrix.sh, pinned to one CPU, 9 repetitions with random interleaving and a 1% CV bar.
corrections.hardware: Raspberry Pi 5 (Cortex-A76, NEON, performance governor); Intel Xeon Platinum 8481C @ 2.70GHz (Sapphire Rapids, cloud vCPU); Intel Xeon @ 2.00GHz (Skylake-SP, GCP vCPU); Intel Xeon @ 2.80GHz Cascade Lake (family 6 model 85 stepping 7) on a 4-vCPU slice and on a whole 2-socket host.
corrections.caveats: Very new (first runs 2026-08), one author, not yet tagged, 0 stars. All numbers are first-party. Cycles per byte uses RDTSC reference cycles (perf_event on the Pi) and only compares within one machine. Per-value operator() on the Pi 5 is 0.87x the speed of std::mt19937; operator() through the refill buffer is 1.5-2.4x slower than generate_n. xoshiro256++ is cheaper per byte on four of the five machines (vphilox wins only on Skylake-SP, 0.4210 vs 0.4703 cycles/byte). Four archived harness-validation runs (unpinned governor, 2-vCPU VM) are excluded from the figures by the project. SIMD backends are checked bit-for-bit against the scalar Random123 reference vectors (tests/test_reference_vectors.cpp, tests/test_kernel_parity.cpp). The accompanying paper is a preprint (TechRxiv/Zenodo), not peer-reviewed. libstdc++ inferred from GCC on Ubuntu/Debian.

notes: All ratios in the record match the table in docs/benchmarks/README.md; README's '1.3x to 4.6x' equals 1/0.75 and 1/0.22. RNG check passed: every SIMD backend must reproduce the scalar Philox4x32-10 stream. Metadata: MIT OR Apache-2.0, 0 stars, 0 forks, 151 commits, default branch master, last commit 2026-08-31.

tier_reason: This is the replication package (TOMACS_RCR) of a peer-reviewed ACM TOMACS 29(1) 2019 paper, and cpp/shuffle.cpp times std::shuffle beside the OpenBSD-like, Java-like and nearly divisionless shuffles on the same lehmer64 generator. The repo states only g++/clang++ with -std=c++11 -O3; the sample output has no CPU or compiler version, and the paper itself could not be opened, so not A.

corrections.caveats: Peer-reviewed paper (ACM TOMACS 2019, 'Fast Random Integer Generation in an Interval') with a replication package, but the numbers on the page are an illustrative sample run ('the exact numbers will vary') with no CPU, compiler version or standard library stated. The std::shuffle baseline reflects libstdc++ before it adopted this very technique in std::uniform_int_distribution, so the gap against a current libstdc++ is smaller. The benchmark generator is lehmer64, not std::mt19937, so the std::shuffle column isolates the range-reduction and shuffle cost. In the RCR gnuplot script, Figure 3a (shuffle32.pdf) plots the std::shuffle series from the 64-bit rows ('every 2::1'), which understates std::shuffle's 32-bit cost in that figure. The repo Makefile uses -O3 without -march. Last commit 2024-03-12.

notes: Sample numbers at size 10000 (32-bit: 1.80 / 5.32 / 2.98 / 18.57; 64-bit: 1.78 / 14.40 / 7.97 / 15.23) match TOMACS_RCR/README.md; INCLUDESTDSHUFFLE is defined, so the std::shuffle column is live. A WebSearch summary (paper not opened; arXiv, ACM DL and lemire.me are blocked) says the paper used an Intel i7-6700 with GCC 5.4 -O3 -march=native and found std::shuffle close to the OpenBSD-like method; if confirmed, this could be retiered to A with that paper as benchmark_url. Not a duplicate of cpp_batched_random (the later batched technique, already listed). Metadata: Apache-2.0, 41 stars, 5 forks, 56 commits; stale.

tier_reason: The README table (CPU time for 1e9 outputs, gcc -O3, i7-3770 and Phenom II X6 1045T) is first-party. The repo has no timing harness (melg19937-64.c's main only prints sample outputs) and no compiler version. The peer-reviewed ACM TOMS paper could not be opened, and its abstract claims 'speeds equivalent to 64-bit Mersenne Twisters', not a win, so B is not supported.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README table, CPU seconds for 1e9 64-bit outputs: MELG19937-64 4.2123 (Intel Core i7-3770) / 6.2920 (AMD Phenom II X6 1045T) vs reference MT19937-64 5.1002 / 6.6490 (about 1.21x and 1.06x, derived from page data). SFMT19937-64 without SIMD is about level (4.2654 / 5.6123, faster on the AMD part) and with SIMD much faster (1.8457 / 2.8806). The README and paper describe the speed as 'equivalent to' / 'competitive with' MT19937-64; the claimed advantage is equidistribution (Delta=0 vs 7820 for MT19937-64).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc with -O3 on Linux (README Platforms section); compiler version not stated; build line 'gcc melg19937-64.c -o melg19937-64 -O3 -Wall'. No timing program is in the repo.
corrections.caveats: Speed is parity-class, not a speedup: about 6-21% faster than the reference mt19937-64.c and slower than SFMT19937-64 without SIMD on the AMD part. No public timing harness, no compiler version, 2012-era CPUs. std::mt19937_64 itself was not measured; in VMT19937's tables (another project, other CPUs) libstdc++'s std::mt19937_64 runs 1.17-1.76x faster than the same reference mt19937-64.c, so a win over std::mt19937_64 is not shown. ACM TOMS 2018 paper (Harase and Kimoto) cited but not opened. Value is equidistribution quality (maximally equidistributed, N1=9603). Last commit 2023-03-18.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly. Downgraded B to C: the paper's abstract (seen only in a WebSearch summary; ACM DL, arXiv and the author's site are blocked) claims equivalent speed, and the repo has no timing code. Kept rather than rejected because the table does show it ahead of MT19937-64; record 'not faster than std::mt19937_64 shown' as the shortcoming. Metadata: MIT (LICENSE.md, 2021), 15 stars, 3 forks, 35 commits; abandoned (>3 years).
